The '''Buriganga River''' ({{lang-bn|বুড়িগঙ্গা}}, ''Buŗigônga'', {{translation|"Old [[Ganges]]"}}) is a river in [[Bangladesh]] which flows past the southwest outskirts of the capital city, [[Dhaka]]. Its average depth is {{convert|25|ft|m|disp=flip}} and its maximum depth is {{convert|58|ft|m|disp=flip}}. It ranks among the most [[water pollution|polluted]] rivers in the country.<ref name="Majumder 2009">{{cite web |last=Majumder |first=Azad |title=Bangladesh river pollution threatens millions |work=Reuters |date=19 May 2009 |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-bangladesh-rivers-idUSTRE54I04G20090519 |access-date=9 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="the Guardian 2015">{{cite web |title=The river runs black: pollution from Bangladesh's tanneries – in pictures |website=the Guardian |date=23 October 2015 |url=http://www.theguardian.com/global-development-professionals-network/gallery/2015/oct/23/the-river-runs-black-pollution-from-bangladeshs-tanneries-in-pictures |access-date=9 January 2020}}</ref>

==Dhaleshwari River==
[[File:Dhaka River Scenery 1875.jpg|thumb|250px|left|View looking along the river Buriganga towards the city of Dhaka situated on the left bank. A Hindu temple tower stands at the water's edge (1875).]]
According to [[R. C. Majumdar]], in the distant past, it is probable that a course of the [[Ganges]] river used to reach the [[Bay of Bengal]] through the [[Dhaleshwari River]]. The Buriganga originated from the [[Dhaleshwari River|Dhaleshwari]] in the south of Savar, near Dhaka <ref>{{cite book |last=Majumdar |first=R. C. |author-link=R. C. Majumdar |year=1971 |title=History of Ancient Bengal |location=Calcutta |publisher=G. Bhardwaj & Co. |page=3 |oclc=961157849}}.</ref> In the 20th century the water table and river became polluted by [[polythenes]]{{clarify|date=January 2020}} and other hazardous substances from demolished buildings near the river banks.

==Pollution==
[[File:Buriganga 1.jpg|thumb|View of the Buriganga river at Sadarghat area with some launches.]]
The Buriganga is economically very important to Dhaka. [[launch (boat)|Launch]]es and country boats provide connection to other parts of [[Bangladesh]], a largely riverine country. When the Mughals made Dhaka their capital in 1610, the banks of the Buriganga were already a prime location for trade. The river was also the city's main source of drinking water.

Today, the Buriganga river is afflicted by the noisome problem of pollution. The chemical waste of mills and factories, household waste, [[medical waste]], [[sewage]], dead animals, [[plastic pollution|plastics]], and oil are some of the Buriganga's pollutants. The city of Dhaka discharges about 4,500 tons of [[solid waste]] every day and most of it is released into the Buriganga.{{Citation needed|date=September 2011}} According to the [[Ministry of Environment and Forest (Bangladesh)|Department of Environment]], {{convert|21600|m3|e6USgal|abbr=off}} of [[toxic waste]] are released into the river by the [[tanneries]] every day.<ref>{{cite magazine |date=25 October 2002 |title=Pollution control and tannery relocation |url=http://www.leathermag.com/features/featurepollution-control-and-tannery-relocation/ |magazine=Leather International |publisher=Global Trade Media |access-date=22 February 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.hrw.org/report/2012/10/08/toxic-tanneries/health-repercussions-bangladeshs-hazaribagh-leather |title=Toxic Tanneries: The Health Repercussions of Bangladesh's Hazaribagh Leather |date=8 October 2012 |website=Human Rights Watch |access-date=22 February 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Aulakh |first=Raveena |date=12 October 2013 |title=Bangladesh's tanneries make the sweatshops look good |url=https://www.thestar.com/news/world/clothesonyourback/2013/10/12/bangladeshs_tanneries_make_the_sweatshops_look_good.html |newspaper=Toronto Star |access-date=22 February 2017}}</ref> Experts identified nine industrial areas in and around the capital city as the primary sources of river pollution: [[Tongi]], [[Tejgaon Thana|Tejgaon]], [[Hazaribagh Thana|Hazaribagh]], Tarabo, [[Narayanganj]], [[Savar Upazila|Savar]], [[Gazipur City|Gazipur]], Dhaka Export Processing Zone and Ghorashal. Most of the industrial units of these areas have no sewage treatment or [[effluent treatment plant]]s (ETPs) of their own.

[[File:Buriganga River, Dhaka.jpg|thumb|6000px|centre|View of Buriganga River from the bridge in Dhaka]]

More than {{convert|60000|m3|cuft}} of toxic waste, including [[textile]] [[dyeing]], printing, washing and pharmaceuticals, are released into the main water bodies of Dhaka every day.{{Citation needed|date=September 2011}} According to the Dhaka Water and Sewerage Authority (WASA), about {{convert|12000|m3|cuft}} of untreated waste are released into the lake from [[Tejgaon Industrial Area Thana|Tejgaon]], [[Badda Thana|Badda]] and [[Mohakhali]] industrial areas every day. The waste mostly comes from [[garment washing]] and [[dyeing plant]]s. [[Textile industries]] annually discharge as much as 56 million tonnes of waste and 0.5 million tonnes of sludge. Sewage is also released into the Buriganga. A newspaper article from 2004<ref>{{cite news |title=Dhaka's looming water crisis |url=http://www.financialexpress-bd.com/index3.asp?cnd=2/25/2005&section_id=4&newsid=13499&spcl=no |newspaper=The Financial Express |location=Dhaka |type=Editorial |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050310182755/http://www.financialexpress-bd.com/index3.asp?cnd=2%2F25%2F2005&section_id=4&newsid=13499&spcl=no |archive-date=10 March 2005 |url-status=dead }}</ref> indicated that up to 80% of Dhaka's sewage was untreated. Because of Dhaka's heavy reliance on river transport for goods, including food, the Buriganga receives especially high amounts of [[food waste]] since unusable or rotting portions of fruits, vegetables, and fish are thrown into the river.

Nearly 4.0 million people of the city are exposed to the consequences of water pollution every day.{{Citation needed|date=September 2011}}
